articles.title: From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
articles.summary: In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case. While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been…
body: That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Acclaim and box office success are raising the possibility that a documentary could finally break one of the Academy’s longest-standing barriers. If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic. But it would also raise an uncomfortable question: Why did it take this long?
To celebrate this potential historic nomination, Variety is ranking the 20 films that should have received a best picture nomination in the past 40 years.

The films mentioned here span genres, styles and subjects, from the pursuit of an NBA dream to a high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers, from a confrontation with Indonesia’s history of mass killing to a real-time account of Edward Snowden’s revelations.
You can blame the Academy at large for some of these omissions; others tie directly to the Documentary Branch itself, which snubbed many of them in its own category.
points: In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture.
That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.
If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic.

articles.title: James Gunn Defends the DC Universe, Says He Dislikes the Idea That ‘Individual Stories Aren’t Meaningful Unless They Lead to Something’
articles.summary: James Gunn took to Threads on Saturday to defend the DCU and his decision to expand the universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event.
body: In the post that Gunn responded to, the user had replied to an image that listed out his DC Universe foundation — “Superman,” “Peacemaker,” “Supergirl,” “Creature Commandos,” “Clayface” and “Lanters” — followed by the text: “What is this building towards???”

“Clayface,” which his theaters on Friday, is Gunn’s latest DCU installment, following 2025’s “Superman” and this year’s “Supergirl.” (Ahead of the film’s release, comic fans pointed out that the character, who has never been the subject of a standalone feature film, is a considerably nicher choice than previous DCU films.) It generated $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, comfortably taking the No. 1 spot at the box office.

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star.

articles.title: ‘He’s not going to punk me. I’ll trick him’: Ali G: Who Iz I? stooge says he was in on joke but didn’t tell Sacha Baron Cohen
articles.summary: Exclusive: Joshua Loudermilk says suspicions first raised during filming by gun shaped like wearable plastic bottom: ‘You’re gonna put a butt on top of a butt? You can’t run in that’ • This article contains spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?
body: Joshua Loudermilk, one of two men apparently discredited by the new Ali G movie Ali G: Who Iz I?, has said that he was in on the joke, but that the film-makers didn’t realise this.

Loudermilk, a 54-year-old aspiring actor from North Carolina, has told the Guardian he recognised star Sacha Baron Cohen early in the shoot but continued pretending to be a hard-right Maga sympathiser prepared to defend the US border at all costs.

The movie involves Loudermilk being recruited by another Cohen character, the ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, to help form a citizens’ warrior force to protect US borders, making use of his top-secret new weapon: a gun disguised as buttocks.

Along with fellow recruit Michael Aboud, the chair of the El Paso county Republican party, Loudermilk joins Morad on a mission to stop the birth on US soil of the baby of a fictional South American drugs kinpin. This involves abducting a woman apparently in labour, abandoning her in a deserted medical facility, kidnapping her newborn child (a lifelike prosthetic) and driving it in a zipped bag to the border in order to deliver it by drone to Mexico.

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Director Lance Oppenheim Says Billy Evans ‘Didn’t Care About Being Seen Naked’; Evans Asked, ‘Want to Film Me Showering?’
articles.summary: “You Can See Everything” audiences were expecting to be taken aback for a variety of reasons when watching the documentary, but a full-frontal shot of Elizabeth Holmes’ partner Billy Evans wasn’t something many foresaw experiencing in the theater.
body: “So I don’t know what that means, but I feel like there’s enough stuff in there that gives me the impression that maybe he was excited that people could see everything and that there was full access, I guess,” Oppenheim continued. “But it really beats me, honestly. We were in the car ride on the way back from the gym, and I said to Billy, ‘We will give you some time to shower.’ And Billy responded, ‘Want to film me showering?’ I offered to film him in a way that could avoid seeing his genitals, but Billy said he didn’t care about being seen naked.”

Ahead of the film’s release earlier this month, Evans admitted he hadn’t seen the doc while appearing on the “All-In” podcast. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said on the podcast, admitting that Holmes “looks insane” in the trailer.

Before hitting theaters on Oct. 16, “You Can See Everything” had been quietly in the works from Fielder and Oppenheim for more than three years. The doc offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

articles.title: Peggy King, ‘George Gobel Show’ Actress and Singer of the ’50s, Dies at 96
articles.summary: Peggy King, a 1950s television and recording star, died Sunday following a battle with Alzheimer’s at the Saunders House Assisted Living facility in Wynnewood, Pa. She was 96. King’s publicist, Alan Eicher, confirmed her death. King was a regular on the “George Gobel Show” from 1954-57.
body: In 1952, she signed to an MGM contract, which led to a cameo in Vincente Minnelli’s “The Bad and the Beautiful,” in which she sang on the soundtrack album. She also appeared in “Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy.”

Mitch Miller signed her to a long-term contract with Columbia Records, where she made two best-selling albums. She had a string of hit singles, and composer Arthur Hamilton wrote “Cry Me a River” for her but Miller would not let her record the song.

King starred with Tab Hunter in the television musical “Hans Brinker or the Silver Skates.” She also starred in a TV musical version of “Jack and the Beanstalk” with Joel Grey, Celeste Holm and Cyril Ritchard. She played a stewardess in the 1957 thriller “Zero Hour!” with Dana Andrews and Linda Danell.

She was inducted into the Broadcast Pioneers Hall of Fame in 2010 and was among the first celebrities honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. King’s last released recording was the album “Songs a la King,” released in 2016. She performed regularly in the Philadelphia area, New York and Los Angeles as late as 2014.

articles.title: Spotify uploads lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene in Irish
articles.summary: The single is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.
body: The lyrics to Dolly Parton's Welsh version of her hit Jolene were uploaded mistakenly to Spotify in Irish.
The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.
The version has parts of the song sung in English and Welsh - but the lyrics presented on the digital audio streaming service Spotify actually showed the language as Irish.
Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment.

articles.title: An Underrated Batman Cartoon Has The Most Tragic Version Of Clayface
articles.summary: The Batman, an animated series that debuted in 2004, features a tragic version of Clayface that brings another Caped Crusader villain to mind.
body: Clayface is a Batman villain built for animation. He exists as a writhing mass of living mud that can take any shape he can think of, and animation offers motion that comics don't while also limiting artists' imagination far less than live-action. DC Studios' new horror movie "Clayface" takes after the villain's debut appearance in "Batman: The Animated Series," "Feat of Clay," because that's the gold standard for a Clayface origin story.

"Batman: The Animated Series" is the superlative version of the Dark Knight and his villains, but I'd argue another Batman cartoon did a fine job with its Clayface — while going even further in reinventing him. That would be 2004's "The Batman." It lived in the shadow of "The Animated Series," and despite being a younger show, it's not as remembered, yet "The Batman" staked out a unique identity with lots of great episodes. A lot of that verve came from art director and character designer Jeff Matsuda ("Jackie Chan Adventures"). He utilized a more anime-esque art style compared to Bruce Timm's Fleischer "Superman"-inspired classicism on "Batman: The Animated Series."

articles.title: Why Akuma From Street Fighter (2026) Looks So Familiar
articles.summary: If you saw the 2026 Street Fighter movie and thought you recognized Akuma but couldn't place where you'd seen him before, this is written specifically for you.
body: The latest attempt to turn "Street Fighter" into a blockbuster movie franchise is here. Hollywood and Capcom have tried (and failed) at various points to turn the beloved fighting games into successful cinematic adaptations before. Some people believe that 1994's "Street Fighter" is actually good, but I think we can all agree that the less said about "Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li," the better. Paramount and Legendary, however, have assembled one heck of a cast for this latest iteration — some of whom should look familiar to audiences.

M. Bison from "Street Fighter" looks familiar, as he's played by beloved character actor David Dastmalchian, and he's the main villain of the movie. However, the third act fully introduces us to Akuma, another villain who has been lurking in the shadows. Heavily cloaked in makeup and CGI, it may be hard to make out which actor is bringing the villain to life, but he's a familiar presence in the world of entertainment.

articles.title: Star Trek's Brent Spiner Won't Take Credit For Data's Most Important Contribution [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Brent Spiner, who played the android Data in the Star Trek franchise, tells us that he refuses to take credit for a big part of the reaction to his character.
body: While the "Blade Runner" franchise gets all the credit for its themes about becoming "more human than human," "Star Trek" has always been on the bleeding edge of this classic sci-fi concern. Spock, of course, symbolizes the franchise's most enduring attempt to reflect our own intrinsic foibles and eccentricities throughout "The Original Series" and beyond. But coming in a close second place would have to be Brent Spiner's Data, the lovable android who's devoted much of his programming to the pursuit of making sense of his flesh-and-blood crewmates.

The legacy of Data extends far beyond the mediums of film and television, however. Countless fans have come to view the scene-stealer of "The Next Generation" as an avatar for basic human rights, coexistence, and, most intriguingly of all, neurodivergence. It's easy to see why. As someone on the outside looking in at an entire world of emotions and feelings — which he logically intuits, but struggles to regulate and understand — Data's journey has struck a chord with anyone who's gone through similar experiences in life.
